description: Five visitor-accessible rounds in and around Orlando: a championship test at Orange County National, Disney's historic Magnolia course, Greg Norman's links-style International at ChampionsGate, Jack Nicklaus's St. Andrews tribute at Grand Cypress, and the water-laden Shingle Creek course near the convention corridor.
intro: Orlando is better known for theme parks than for golf, which is exactly why it works so well as a golf trip: the courses are built for visitors, the season runs all year, and you can pair a morning round with an afternoon at the parks without changing hotels. The five courses below are all open to traveling golfers — public or resort courses you can book without a membership — and together they cover the full Central Florida range, from a links-style test to a historic parkland layout. Base yourself near Lake Buena Vista or International Drive and none of them is more than about half an hour away.

sections.heading: 1. Orange County National — Panther Lake, Winter Garden
paragraphs: Panther Lake is the original course at Orange County National, a golf-only facility west of Orlando in Winter Garden, and the purest championship test on this list. Designed by Phil Ritson, Dave Harman and Isao Aoki and opened in 1997, the par-72 layout winds through rolling meadows, native pines, wetlands and lakes, with elevation changes of up to 60 feet — rare for Florida — and no housing lining the holes. Orange County National has hosted PGA Tour Q-School finals, and the property's 42-acre, 360-degree practice facility is one of the largest in the country.

Make this your anchor round and the first tee time you book, since it draws serious golfers from everywhere and rewards a fresh swing. The multiple tee options keep it playable for mid-handicaps, but pick an honest set: the back tees are a genuine championship test. Pair it with its links-style sibling, Crooked Cat, on the same property for a 36-hole day, and leave time for the practice facility — it is worth a visit in its own right.

sections.heading: 2. Disney's Magnolia Golf Course, Lake Buena Vista
paragraphs: Disney's Magnolia Golf Course opened on October 1, 1971, the same day the Magic Kingdom opened, and it is the most storied resort course in Orlando. Designed by Joe Lee, it hosted the PGA Tour's Walt Disney World Golf Classic from 1971 through 2012, and it was recently reimagined with reconstructed greens, rebuilt teeing grounds and new sandy waste areas, with four holes rerouted. The course is named for its more than 1,500 magnolia trees, and its par-3 sixth hole features a bunker shaped like Mickey Mouse — the Mouse Trap.

This is the round to play if your trip mixes golf with the parks: it sits across from Disney's Grand Floridian Resort, so you can walk off the course and straight into a resort day. Book it early in the trip rather than saving it for last, when park fatigue sets in, and play it from a comfortable tee — at over 7,500 yards from the back, it is the longest of Disney's courses. Families splitting time between golf and the parks will find this the easiest sell in the group.

sections.heading: 3. ChampionsGate Golf Club — International Course, ChampionsGate
paragraphs: The International Course at ChampionsGate is the closest thing to British links golf in Central Florida. Designed by Greg Norman and opened in 2000, then remodeled by Norman in 2016, it is a broad, windswept links-style layout at the Omni Orlando Resort, with wide fairways, huge greens, some 150 bunkers and water lurking beside many holes. Golf Digest lists it as a public facility, and its sister course, the National, offers a more traditional tree-lined Florida test on the same property.

Play the International on a day when you want a different kind of challenge from the rest of the trip — wind, firm turf and bump-and-run shots rather than target golf over water. The short par-4 12th is the classic risk-reward hole, so take the aggressive line only if you can live with the bunker. Because it sits just southwest of Disney World, it pairs naturally with a Magnolia round the day before or after for a resort-golf double.

sections.heading: 4. Grand Cypress Golf — Links Course, Orlando
paragraphs: Grand Cypress's Links Course — opened in 1988 as the New Course — is Jack Nicklaus's tribute to the Old Course at St. Andrews, set in an open meadow at Evermore Orlando Resort. The design borrows the original's signatures: double greens, stone bridges and walls, gorse mounds, burns, and pot bunkers as deep as 12 feet, more than 150 of them across the course. Both the Cypress and Links courses are open to resort guests and the public, with non-resort guests able to book tee times up to 60 days in advance, based on availability.

This is the fun round of the trip, and the one to play when the group wants a break from Florida water hazards — very little water comes into play here. The generous fairways invite driver, but the pot bunkers punish misses, so favor position over distance and practice a low running shot before you arrive. Book inside the 60-day window as soon as it opens if you are not staying at the resort, and pair it with the parkland Cypress Course for a two-course day on one property.

sections.heading: 5. Shingle Creek Golf Club, Orlando
paragraphs: Shingle Creek Golf Club is the convention corridor's championship course, and the hardest test on this list for many visitors. First designed by David Harmon in 2003 and redesigned in 2016 by Thad Layton of the Arnold Palmer Design Company, the par-72 layout sits at the headwaters of the Everglades, with interconnected hazards bringing water into play on 15 holes, elevated greens and closely mown run-offs that invite creative short-game shots. It is the closest course to the Orange County Convention Center and minutes from International Drive, Universal Orlando and Disney World.

Save Shingle Creek for the middle of the trip, once you have a round or two under your belt — the redesign softened the original, but water on 15 holes still demands respect. Play from a tee that lets you carry the hazards comfortably rather than the back tees, and bring extra balls. Its location makes it the perfect final round before a flight home, or the easy add-on round for a convention trip when you only have one free morning.
